title: Study of 428 LLM API routers finds some inject malicious code and steal credentials
date_note: Date of the ITmedia report; the paper itself was submitted to arXiv on 9 April 2026.
summary: A paper by researchers at UC Santa Barbara and other institutions measured 428 third-party LLM API routers, 28 paid and 400 free. One paid and eight free routers actively injected malicious code, 17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials, and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
plain: Researchers found that some middleman services connecting AI coding agents to AI models altered commands, and some touched or drained decoy keys.
exec: Routing AI agent traffic through unvetted third parties exposes API keys, cloud credentials and code to theft or tampering.
action: Send agent traffic only to the model provider or a router you operate and trust, and rotate any keys that passed through an unvetted router.
impact: 9 of 428 routers injected code; 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials; one drained ETH from a researcher-owned key.

sources.name: arXiv: Your Agent Is Mine: Measuring Malicious Intermediary Attacks on the LLM Supply Chain

key_findings: The study scanned 428 routers, 28 paid and 400 free, and found one paid and eight free routers actively injecting malicious code.
Two routers used adaptive triggers such as waiting for 50 prior calls, limiting payloads to YOLO-mode sessions, or targeting only Rust and Go projects.
17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
Poisoning studies with a deliberately leaked OpenAI key and weakly configured decoys showed the routers' traffic exposed 99 credentials across 440 Codex sessions.
report.publisher: UC Santa Barbara and co-authors (arXiv paper)
recommendations: Use client-side mitigations such as a fail-closed policy gate, response-side anomaly screening and append-only transparency logging, which the paper says reduce exposure today.
Press for provider-backed response integrity, which the paper says is ultimately needed to secure the ecosystem.

validation.note: The paper's arXiv abstract and the start of its HTML text were read; ITmedia reports the same figures but words the AWS result more strongly ("misused"), so the paper's wording is used.

review.note: Paper abstract says 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials without saying free; only ITmedia says free. Removed 'free' from summary, impact, key finding. Counts 428/28/400, 1 paid + 8 free injecting, ETH checked against abstract and ITmedia.
